business.title: Graphene-enhanced biochar membrane boosts thermal storage and moisture control for ventilation systems
business.desc: Researchers at Yonsei University, National University of Singapore and Dankook University have developed a paper membrane that combines food-waste-derived biochar, graphene, and a phase-change material to simultaneously store thermal energy, improve heat transfer, and manage moisture - aimed at energy-recovery ventilation and other building thermal-management systems. Phase-change materials (PCMs) are attractive for thermal energy storage because they absorb heat as they melt and release it as they solidify, but conventional PCMs are limited by low thermal conductivity and a tendency to leak during melting. To address this, the team produced biochar from mixed food waste carbonized at 400°C, then activated it with potassium hydroxide at temperatures between 600°C and 800°C. A small amount of graphene - roughly 1% by weight - was then coated onto the biochar via ultrasonication to widen its pore structure and improve conductivity, before the resulting porous carbon was infiltrated with docosane, a paraffin-based PCM, to form the composite. The biochar activated at 700°C performed best, with a surface area of 323.1 m2/g and a mesopore proportion of 82.8%, providing ample space to hold the PCM while helping prevent leakage. Adding graphene to this engineered biochar increased latent heat storage by up to 72.0% compared with the non-graphitized composite, reaching a phase-change enthalpy of 93.1 J/g at around 48.4°C, and the composite retained roughly 90.2% of that enthalpy after 1,000 heating-cooling cycles - equivalent to the researchers' estimate of about three years of ventilation-system operation.When bonded to a commercial paper membrane, the composite raised thermal conductivity by 96.1% relative to a pristine reference membrane while retaining 80.2% of the bulk composite's latent heat. Despite the added conductivity, moisture permeability remained strong, with the membrane meeting ISO 12572 requirements and posting an equivalent air-layer thickness of 0.71 - below the 1.0 threshold considered permeable.
